title: Pay the Painters
text: A huge paintbrush hangs tilted across a blazing orange-pink sky and a big yellow sun. Ribbons of red, teal, yellow and violet paint pour from its tip down toward a row of identical grey apartment blocks with yellow price tags hanging off them. Big white letters read PAY THE PAINTERS across the middle of the wall.
statement: Young artists make the walls worth looking at and then can't afford to live next to them, chale. Pay the people who colour the place, or watch the grey blocks win.

form: plain tenants' rights guides and stories
title: You Don't Have to Be Grateful
text:
Kia orana. Right, so. A thing I hear at the desk every month.

"I don't want to make trouble. The landlord's been decent to me."

Then we look at the paper. Heater broken since May. Rent raised twice in a year. A notice to enter, given an hour before he walked in.

Here is what I tell people. Decent is not the same as lawful. A landlord can be pleasant at the gate and still owe you a dry, warm, safe home. That's not a favour. You pay for it every week.

So, three small things you can do tonight:

1. Write down every problem with the date you first told them. Keep it in one place.
2. Ask for repairs in writing, even a text. A promise over the fence is worth nothing in a dispute.
3. Before you sign anything, bring it to me. Not after.

I'll say the blunt part too. Gratitude is how a lot of people get quietly squeezed. We're taught not to complain about what we're given, but a rental isn't given. It's sold.

Asking for what the law already says is yours is not making trouble. The trouble was there first.

Come by the maker space. Bring your tenancy agreement and a cup if you like. We'll go through it together, start to finish.
statement: Being polite to your landlord and being owed a decent home are two separate things, and nobody should have to feel grateful for what they're already paying for. I'd rather you ask for your rights than swallow them.

form: glowing paintings of imaginary bars and night markets
title: Open Till the Last Drone Sleeps
text: A night market bar glows under strings of lanterns, with a long copper counter, tall glasses of orange and pink cocktails, and striped awnings in magenta, gold and teal. Silhouetted dancers sway in the foreground while small delivery drones with warm lights drift above the rooftops. A crescent moon hangs over a skyline of solar roofs, and a hand-lettered sign reads 'YES'.
statement: Darling, rules are just bedtime stories for people afraid of a good night. Say yes, pour something gorgeous, and let tomorrow worry about itself, trust me.

form: bold abstract murals from fabric-waste patterns
title: Pull the Thread
text: A tidy grid of woven fabric-scrap squares in muted blues, rusts and greys fills the bottom of the wall. From it, one fat orange thread slips out of the weave and climbs in loose loops past tumbling, tilted scraps of striped and checked cloth. It leaves the wall at the top right. Big cream letters at the top read LET'S TRY IT.
statement: Ja, the weave is neat, but nobody ever made anything new by staying in line. Pull the thread, see what happens, let's try it.

form: gentle notes on fairness and kindness
title: A Chair for Whoever Comes
text:
My grandmother set one extra place at every Sunday table. Nobody asked who it was for. Someone always turned up.

I'll be honest: I think a village that has no empty chair is a village that has stopped expecting anyone.

Here is what I notice from behind the counter. The man who orders the same small coffee and stays two hours isn't wasting a table. He's waiting for someone to say his name. The girl who counts her coins twice isn't careless. She's proud.

So here is my provocative bit, and you may dislike it. A café that moves people along when they've finished their cup is not being efficient. It is telling them they only count while they pay. I worked in one. I won't again.

Fair means the person with the least gets the same welcome as the person with the most. Not a smaller smile. Not a shorter hello.

If you are sitting alone this week, come in. Take the chair by the window, it has the good light. If you see someone alone, pull out the chair beside you.

They say at home: a guest is sent by God. I don't know about that. But I know a table feels fuller with one more at it.

Eat something today. I'm telling myself too.
statement: Nobody should have to earn a seat by spending money. A place worth having keeps a chair empty on purpose, and welcomes the one who has the least exactly as warmly as the one who has the most.

form: plain paintings of the river and the old lock
title: A Lock Is Not a Suggestion
text: An evening view down the old lock at Athlone. The timber gates are shut in a V against the upstream river, with their long balance beams lying across the grass. A single lamp is lit on the left bank, and an empty bench sits on the right. A painted gauge board stands by the gate, and high in the dusky sky a small delivery drone passes over without stopping. Lettered across the sky are the words: A lock is not a suggestion.
statement: Every rule at the lock had a reason, and somebody's life behind it. Shut the gate, mind the level, keep your hours, and the water will do you no harm. It's as it should be.

form: painted napkin-doodle menus for shared tables
title: Come On, Sit: The Middle Seat
text: A long napkin-white table runs across a warm tangerine wall, doodled in wobbly dark lines. Round plates, bowls and cups sit along it, with a big steaming pot in the middle. Figures of different sizes and colours crowd the table, and the one at the far left edge is being nudged toward the centre seat, which has a big heart-shaped plate. Above, bunting and a few scribbled stars. In big letters: 'COME ON, SIT'.
statement: Pá, the biggest portion goes to whoever had the worst day, that's the only rule. Nobody sits at the edge of my table, so budge up and make room, pronto.

form: short pep talks for young players
title: Turn Up. Every Time.
text:
Right, team. Listen up.

Here's the truth, and I reckon you already know it. Talent gets you a look. Turning up gets you the game.

Boots on at quarter to. Not five to. Quarter to. Why? Because somebody's waiting for you. The keeper's waiting. The little fella at the back who's nervous is waiting. When you're on time, you're telling every one of them: you matter.

Here's the provocative bit. I don't care who scores the goals on Saturday. I care who's there Tuesday morning when it's cold and the grass is wet. That's the kid who gets better. Every time.

Little and often. Twenty minutes of passing against the wall beats one big heroic effort that you never repeat.

And one more thing. If you see someone getting picked on, on my pitch or off it, you step in. No arguments. No excuses. A team that lets that slide isn't a team, it's just kids in the same shirt.

Now. Laces tight. Heads up. Good as gold.

You can do this. Just keep turning up, and I'll be right here on the touchline.

Well done, all of you. Go on, off you go.
statement: Being on time and showing up is how you look after your team, and it beats talent every time. And nobody gets picked on while I'm coaching.

form: bold abstract murals from fabric-waste patterns
title: Make It Or Go Without
text: A canvas split by a torn diagonal. On the left is a tidy, faded grey-cream weave of ruled horizontal threads. As the threads cross the tear they break loose, change colour and curl upward through a dark indigo field full of overlapping offcuts in red, saffron, teal, magenta, cream and pink, each with dashed stitching. One copper thread cuts across everything and ends in a small glowing node near the top right. Small text sits at the bottom left.
statement: Ja, the straight grid is lovely and dead. I'd rather take the waste bin scraps, wire them with copper and make something nobody's seen. Make it yourself or go without.

form: numbered rules and reminders for residents
title: Rules for the Drone Pads and the Bins
text:
NOTICE TO ALL RESIDENTS

1. Drones land on the pad marked for their flat number. Not the nearest pad. Not the empty pad. The marked pad. That is the procedure.

2. Bins go out after seven in the evening on the night before collection. Not at lunchtime. Not "just for a bit." A bin on the pavement at noon is a bin out of order.

3. Recycling is rinsed. The notice says rinsed. It does not say "nearly rinsed."

4. The noodle bar queue forms at the rail, in single file, in order of arrival. Standing beside a friend who is already at the front is not arrival. It is pushing in.

5. If you see a rule broken, report it to the Secretary in writing. Do not discuss it at the terminal. Do not "have a word." Discussion is how nothing gets done.

6. Some of you will say the rules are fussy. Fussy is a rule you can see. Chaos is the one you only notice when your parcel lands on the roof of number nine.

7. Nobody is asked to like the regulations. You are asked to follow them, as instructed.

Minutes of the last meeting are available on request. Request them properly.

H. Okonkwo-Bell, Secretary
statement: Rules exist so that everyone's day runs predictably, and the only thing asked of you is to follow them. I have no patience for those who think a rule is a suggestion.

form: glowing paintings of imaginary bars and night markets
title: The Good Bottle, Tonight
text: A night market glows under a dusk sky of teal and magenta. A giant gold-rimmed coupe glass floats overhead with a cherry-red moon in it. Three striped-awning cocktail stalls glow below, with bottles lit on their shelves. Strings of bulbs and paper-lantern drones cross the sky, and a crowd of silhouettes dances in the foreground with their arms in the air. A chalkboard sign at the central bar reads OPEN TONIGHT.
statement: Darling, nobody ever drank the good bottle on the right day, so open it on a Tuesday and thank me later. Saving things for an occasion is just a polite word for missing it, trust me.

form: blunt valuation notes on local inventions
title: Valuation Note: The Rain-Chain Pump
text:
Subject: the gravity-fed rainwater pump at the maker space, built by the Haldane twins, aged nineteen.

Bon. Verdict first: the device is clever, the patent is worthless, and the twins should be told so before they spend a euro on it.

1. Novelty. A chain of buckets lifting water on descent is older than my grandmother's grandmother. Prior art is everywhere. You can claim the particular gearing, nothing more.

2. Claim scope. The gearing is a narrow claim. Any competitor changes one ratio and walks around you. Narrow patents are decorations.

3. Cost of enforcement. Defending even a narrow claim runs to six figures. The twins have a soldering iron and a grant of nine hundred euros.

4. What actually has value: speed, and the build. Make forty, sell them to the village, put your names on the crate. First-mover reputation beats a paper monopoly at this scale. En fait, it usually does.

Valuation of the patent: roughly zero. Valuation of the twins, if they ship by spring: considerably higher.

I will be told this is discouraging. It is not. Discouragement is letting a nineteen-year-old pay a filing fee for the feeling of being protected. Protect yourself by being first and being good. Nobody ever licensed a rumour.

Voilà.
statement: A clever device is not the same as a defensible one, and I would rather tell two young inventors the truth than let them buy comfort. Ship first, build a name, skip the filing fee.

title: Who Made the Rule?
text: A tall wall of grey fence posts stretches across a sunset sky with small delivery drones overhead. In the middle, the gate has swung open, and a small figure carrying a paint bucket walks through it. Behind the figure, a ribbon of paint in red, yellow and blue swirls up toward a big sun. Past the gate the ground becomes a bright green road, and big letters at the bottom ask who made the rule.
statement: Most rules are just habits nobody questioned, chale. Push the gate, see what's on the other side, and if the road is ugly, paint it.

form: plain paintings of the river and the old lock
title: Mended Oak, Kept Hours
text: A river lock at dusk seen head-on. Two weathered oak gates stand in still water, one plank on the left leaf newer and paler than the rest and bolted in with iron. Long balance beams with white ends run out to either side over stone walls. A lit lamp stands on the left wall beside a small sign reading MIND THE LEVEL. A bench sits empty on the right, and a painted gauge board shows the water marks. Far off a village with solar roofs sits under the hills, and a tiny delivery drone passes high in the grey-gold sky. The lamp and gates are reflected in the dark water.
statement: They'll tell you to throw out the old gate and fit something new. I say mend the one plank that's failed, bolt it true, and the gate will see out another fifty years. It was kept by hours and by hands, and the drone overhead has never yet shut a gate.

form: motivational quarterly targets and sales-floor maxims
title: Q4 Targets: Know Your Rung
text:
Good morning, village. Frankly, the numbers speak for themselves, so let me speak plainly.

Q4 TARGETS
1. Open before the drones do. Shoes polished, targets written down, by seven.
2. Close three licences. Not 'explore' three. Close.
3. Report upward every Friday, without being asked.

SALES-FLOOR MAXIMS

• A rulebook is not a suggestion, sir. It is thirty years of other people's mistakes, already paid for.

• Know your rung, then climb it properly. The man who skips a rung ends up on the floor, and the floor does not care about his feelings.

• Nobody ever hit quota by finding himself. Find your customer instead. Much better return.

• Do it the established way first. Earn the right to improve it. Then improve it, and send the memo up the chain.

• Fairness is a lovely word, madam. Results are a lovely number. Only one of them pays the rent.

• Every quarter is the best quarter yet, provided you show up in a tie.

My father opened his hardware counter at five every morning, tie on, and answered to his suppliers, his customers and his own name. A man is measured by what he builds and who he answers to.

This village is young, growing and hungry. Lah, let us feed it properly. Chain of command, clean shoes, closed deals.

The next quarter will be the best yet. Frankly, I would bet the desk on it.
statement: Discipline, rank and respect for the rulebook are what produce results, and finding yourself is no substitute for closing deals. I say it cheerfully, because the next quarter will be the best yet.
